Source: docs/performance.md (Performance tuning)

[Aurora](../README.md) / [Documentation](index.md) / Performance

# Measured tuning

Every value here was measured on my own machine before it was kept: a Ryzen 7 5800X with 32 GB of RAM and an RTX 4070
Ti SUPER, on linux-cachyos 7.3.1 (2026-11-04). Your machine may differ, which is why the tuning is optional. `aurora performance on` applies them from [`performance/system/`](../performance/system) and `aurora performance off` puts CachyOS's settings back (`installer/root-steps.sh` `tune` and `untune`, one sudo call each; `./install.sh --performance` does the same as part of an install); the measuring kit is in
[`performance/measure/`](../performance/measure). Re-measure before changing any of them.

## CPU scheduler: scx_lavd (autopilot)

`/etc/scx_loader.toml` (`default_sched = "scx_lavd"`, `default_mode = "Auto"`), `scx_loader.service` enabled,
scx-scheds 1.1.4. On EEVDF every app has its own systemd cgroup at equal weight, so ananicy-cpp's nice values on
compilers never reach other apps; lavd prioritises latency-critical tasks.

Alternating rounds under 32 busy background threads (`performance/measure/probe.py`, `under-load.sh`, `sched/`), with the CPU other
sessions used logged per round:

| | EEVDF | scx_lavd | bpfland | cosmos |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Emoji picker (Win+.) under load | 1099 ms | **666 ms** | 851 ms | 780 ms |
| Konsole under load | 819 ms | **674 ms** | | |
| 7-Zip, scaled to an idle machine | 96-97k MIPS | **101-108k MIPS** | | |
| SCHED_RR 1 ms timer, max | 160 µs | 373 µs (far under a 4.2 ms frame) | | |

lavd `--performance`, flash and p2dq did worse; no scheduler was ejected. BORE ships only as `linux-cachyos-bore`
(a kernel switch, and its 7.3.1 build was broken on 2026-10-31).

## Memory

- **KWin and plasmashell never swap** (`MemorySwapMax=0`, `installer/session/noswap.conf`): with zram and
  CachyOS's swappiness of 150, 795 MB of KWin and Xwayland had been swapped out on 2026-11-04, and switching apps
  stuttered while those pages came back.
- **zram stays** (CachyOS: size = RAM, `vm.swappiness=150` from `/usr/lib/udev/rules.d/30-zram.rules`,
  `page-cluster=0`, zswap off, systemd-oomd active). It is compressed swap inside RAM: 10.3 GB of idle pages held in
  3.3 GB (3.1:1), no OOM kill in 39 h. The kernel docs recommend swappiness above 100 for in-memory swap.
- **`vm.watermark_scale_factor = 125`** (`/etc/sysctl.d/99-aurora-memory.conf`). Before: 244,128 direct-reclaim
  stalls (`allocstall`) and 120,680 early kswapd sleeps (`kswapd_low_wmark_hit_quickly`) in 39 h, the two signs the
  kernel docs give for raising it. In the first 15 minutes after, under the same swap traffic: 0 stalls (about 1,560
  on average before) and 421 early sleeps (about 770). Cost: about 400 MB kept free.
- **zram lz4** (`/etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf.d/90-aurora-zram.conf`, from the next boot). On this CPU with the
  same 64 KiB blocks: decompression 3.7 GB/s (zstd 1.3), compression 717 MB/s (zstd 347); ratio 1.9 against 2.5.
  Cost: about 1 GB more RAM held by zram at 10 GB swapped; under extreme pressure zram's extra room ends sooner.
- KWin and plasmashell have `MemorySwapMax=0` (switching apps used to fault swapped KWin pages back and stutter).
- THP defrag `defer` (`/etc/tmpfiles.d/thp.conf`) after 279k direct-compaction stalls.
- MGLRU `min_ttl_ms` stays at 100: oomd is present.

## Disk I/O scheduler: kyber stays

CachyOS's kyber against ADIOS 3.2.0 on both NVMe disks (2026-11-07, `performance/measure/iosched/ab.py`, results in
`result-2026-11-07.json`): 4 KiB direct random reads timed while two writers stream direct 1 MiB writes, in
alternating 15 s windows. Flat out there was no clean winner; at a realistic load kyber did as well or better.

- nvme0 (ADATA LEGEND 700, `/`): read median under load kyber 954, 3119, 3901 µs against ADIOS 1372, 1402, 1413 µs;
  p99 2.5-10.3 ms against 3.1-7.9 ms. Kyber won the first pair, while the drive was fresh. ADIOS won the later pairs,
  after the drive's write speed fell from 1.24 GB/s to about 0.8 GB/s, and its writers kept more speed (0.9-1.3 GB/s
  against 0.8-1.2).
- nvme1 (Kingston OM8PCP3, `/mnt/D`): the drive's own state ruled. Its writes fell from 618 MB/s to 22 MB/s within
  minutes, and reads stalled up to 0.73 s whichever scheduler ran. ADIOS had the two best loaded windows (p99 0.7 and
  3.7 ms against 25-47 ms for kyber) and also the single worst one (p99 280 ms).
- Unloaded, both read in 77-98 µs at the median. The disk's slowdown under sustained writes costs far more than the
  scheduler choice: builds and downloads on `/mnt/D` stall reads for tens of ms.
- CachyOS keeps ADIOS optional because it is still in development and can lock up in rare cases
  ([wiki](https://wiki.cachyos.org/configuration/general_system_tweaks/)).
- Rerun with a realistic load (`result-2026-11-07-realistic.json`): two buffered writers at 75 MB/s each (150 MB/s,
  a fast download or a build), 20 s of rest before each window, 5 alternating rounds. nvme0: read median 125 µs for
  both; p99 median kyber 455 µs (400-906) against ADIOS 882 µs (409-1407), reads per second 6936 against 6479, kyber
  better in 3 of 5 pairs. nvme1: p99 median kyber 1.5 ms against ADIOS 1.8 ms, reads per second 6055 against 2090,
  kyber better in 3 of 5 pairs; both had windows where the drive stalled (kyber up to 1.1 s, ADIOS up to 0.35 s). At a
  realistic load kyber is as good or better, which settles it.
- The Kingston stalls reads for tens of ms, and once for 1.1 s, even at 150 MB/s of writes and even with the disk
  quiet (p99.9 23 ms). The ADATA never went past 51 ms. Heavy writes belong on the ADATA (`/`, `/home`).

## File Explorer's search

Measured 2026-11-11 on this PC (Ryzen 7 5800X, NVMe btrfs), the helper run as the user with `root = /usr`, 490,544
names, 4 reading threads at idle priority:

| What | Measured |
| --- | --- |
| First index of /usr | 1,125 ms; 3.96 s of CPU over the reading threads |
| Memory | 77.6 MB after the first index; 48.8 MB after a start from the stored index |
| Index file | 21.9 MB |
| Start from the stored index, catch up by folder times | 142 ms |
| A query, a new `aurora-search-query` process each time included (best of 5) | `libQt6Core` 1.9 ms, `python3` 1.9 ms, `kio` 2.6 ms, `.so` 4.6 ms, `ext:h` 11.5 ms, `regex:^lib.*\.so\.6$` 15.5 ms |
| Wakeups in 3 s with a client connected and nothing to do | 0 |

A word is found with one SIMD pass over every name; `ext:`, `regex:` and wildcards test every name, so they grow
with the index (about 5 ms per 100,000 names here). With no client and no work the helper leaves; at rest nothing
runs. The root-only parts (fanotify, the btrfs catch-up) are timed in the virtual machine test: the catch-up after a
restart answered in under 3 s there, the bound the test sets (`tests/vm_server.rs`).

On a data disk, measured 2026-11-11 the same way with `root = /mnt/D` (btrfs, 4,580,100 names, 383,946 folders; one
name in five changes when folded), warm cache, before and after the memory and threading pass:

| What | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First index | 1,956 ms | 1,748 ms |
| Memory after the first index | 545.5 MB | 431.2 MB |
| Start from the stored index (225 MB file) | 1,438 ms, peak 681.9 MB | 1,645 ms, peak 384.5 MB |
| `report` (a word), best of 5, process start included | 10.5 ms | 6.2 ms |
| `ext:pdf` | 93.3 ms | 26.1 ms |
| `regex:^img_[0-9]+\.jpg$` | 124.9 ms | 41.9 ms |

The pass keeps a name as written only when folding changes it, hands freed heap back after a scan (`malloc_trim`),
streams the stored index to and from disk instead of holding a copy of it, and searches in up to 8 threads, one per
16 MiB of folded names (6 here). One thread reads about 12 MiB of folded names per millisecond (the word query alone,
without the 2 ms of process start), so below 32 MiB one thread answers alone.

## Mission Center's glass

Measured in Mission Center's sandbox (`components/mission-center/tools/sandbox`, a nested KWin at 60 Hz, 2026-11-07):
the window on the CPU page over Aurora's wallpaper, 15 s to settle, then the CPU used over 30 s, as a share of one
core. With smooth and sliding graphs on (they redraw every frame), the UI of package 1.2.0.r52-5 and -6 used 20.7 and
19.5 %; -7, whose glass asked GTK for KWin's blur with CSS `backdrop-filter`, used 66.3 % (6.6 % against 4.4 % with
the graphs still). On the desktop's 240 Hz screen it used 52 %. magpie stayed at 4.5 % in every build.

- GTK 4.24 builds `backdrop-filter` into every frame as copy, paste and blur nodes, and to find the region it sends
  KWin it walks the frame (gsk/gskblurutils.c): with a copy around the whole window, it rasterized every clip and graph
  line on the CPU each frame. The workspace's dev build used 66.6 % as it was, 29.3 % without `backdrop-filter` and
  20.1 % with no blur and no tint at all.
- The same nodes around nothing but the paste, from the window's own snapshot, still cost 44.8 %, cached or not: any
  copy node costs every frame.
- Mission Center now keeps GDK off ext-background-effect-v1 (`GDK_WAYLAND_DISABLE`) and asks KWin for the blur itself,
  once per size or state (`src/glass.rs`): 21.4 %, as with no blur. The tint lost its path too: drawn as the sidebar
  card's shadow with no blur, it costs nothing measurable. Package -8, built so: 20.0 % with the graphs animated and
  4.8 % with them still, as before the glass; on the desktop, with the same settings and page, 22 % where -7 used
  52 %.

## Power

- Power profile stays **Performance** (power-profiles-daemon 0.30, amd_pstate EPP; it changes only the CPU's
  EPP/governor). `performance/measure/power/ab.sh` at the same light load: Balanced 44-47 W against 49-56 W package, but the first
  burst after idle 6.1 ms against 5.5 ms (11 % slower). About 7 W, roughly $0.60 a month: not worth it.
- The GPU idles at P5, about 14 W. The CPU package averaged 117 W only while another session's test run used 9 cores.
- Edge tabs playing video hold a "Video Wake Lock" that keeps the screens on.
- Panama's tariff (ASEP, Sept-Dec 2026): above 300 kWh a month the FET subsidy is lost and each extra kWh costs
  $0.23-0.25; a $105 bill is about 500 kWh.

## Display and Edge

- Edge runs on native Wayland (`--ozone-platform=wayland --enable-blink-features=CanvasHDR` in
  `~/.config/microsoft-edge-stable-flags.conf`) for HDR/WCG and exact 240 Hz; computer-use cannot see it there.
- The Samsung DP-1 has VRR "Automatic", not "Always" ("Always" drops the cursor to the content's rate).

# Tests

`scripts/check.sh` builds every part and runs every suite below (about 25 seconds after a build;
`--no-build` skips the build). Counts are those of 2026-11-04 (qmltestrunner counts include its two setup cases).
While working, run the suites of what you changed, once, after the change is written; then the sandbox scenario of the
changed flow.

```bash
export QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen q=/usr/lib/qt6/bin/qmltestrunner B=$PWD/build
```

## Sandbox scenarios

([../docs/sandbox.md](../docs/sandbox.md)). Checking scenarios write PASS or FAIL lines to `tests/sandbox/logs/`; the
others capture `tests/sandbox/shots/` to compare by eye.

| `cli.sh` | the `aurora` command in Konsole with Aurora's profile on Dawn Bird: its menu under the banner and the credit, then `aurora status` (captures) |
| `quick-menu-app-menu.sh` | the app menu: right-click, Pin to Top and the Pinned section, the Menu key (not the field's text menu), Unpin from Dock, an opened app in Suggestions and Remove from Suggestions, no QML warnings (8 PASS); labels found with `tests/helpers/find_text.py` |
| `readme.sh` | the README's pictures, the notifications popover among them (run with `SANDBOX_SCALE=2`, then `assets/screenshots/make.py`, which also crops Mission Center's two from its own sandbox) |
| `kali-menu.sh` | the Kali menu with PC labels |
| `explorer.sh`, `explorer-menus.sh`, `explorer-drives.sh`, `explorer-sidebar-order.sh`, `explorer-crumbs.sh`, `explorer-search.sh`, `explorer-undo.sh`, `explorer-filter.sh`, `explorer-rename.sh`, `explorer-palette.sh`, `explorer-copypaths.sh`, `explorer-inspector.sh`, `explorer-archive.sh`, `explorer-git.sh`, `explorer-columns.sh`, `show-in-folder.sh`, `open-save.sh` | File Explorer, its menus (X11 client), its drives, dragging sidebar rows into a new order, the path segments (clicks, menus, drops, a segment opening under a drag, KIO's menu at the pointer, new tabs; 10 PASS), search from the index (the helper runs as the user on the sandbox's home; 5 PASS with Save to a smart folder and opening it, and the times in logs/search.txt), Undo after Delete (2 PASS), the filter row (3 PASS), the Rename sheet and its Undo (3 PASS), the command palette (3 PASS), Copy Path with several items (1 PASS), the Inspector (3 PASS), archives as folders (2 PASS), Git's status and menu (2 PASS), the columns view (2 PASS), "Show in folder", Open and Save |
| `notifications.sh` | banners in the bottom-right corner, hover buttons |
| `tray-click.sh`, `tray-drag.sh`, `tray-show.sh` | tray clicks, drag to reorder and hide, bring back |
| `control-center.sh`, `control-center-panels.sh`, `control-center-bluetooth.sh`, `control-center-shortcut.sh` | the Control Center, its panels, reopening, its shortcut |
| `dock.sh`, `dock-edge.sh` | the Dock steps aside for a maximized window; one touch of the edge brings it back |
| `pointing-hand.sh`, `pointing-hand-kwin.sh`, `pointing-hand-cost.sh` | the pointing hand in the shell and on window buttons, and its cost |
| `energy-page.sh` | Info Center > Energy after 12 s of samples |
| `menu-bar.sh`, `setup-panels.sh` | the menu bar as installed; the panels from `layout.js` |
| `window-buttons.sh`, `gtk-apps.sh` | the same capsule in KWin-drawn, GTK and libadwaita windows |

## On the live desktop

- `python3 -I components/windows-key/windows_key.py status`; `systemctl --user show -p MainPID --value plasma-krunner.service`.
- `performance/measure/power/ab.sh 3 20` (Balanced against Performance); `performance/measure/probe.py` (launch times).

[Aurora](../README.md) / [Documentation](index.md) / Sandbox

# The sandbox

`tests/sandbox/run.sh SCENARIO [TIMEOUT]` starts an isolated headless Plasma: `kwin_wayland --virtual` (2560x1440,
socket `wayland-sbx`, Xwayland) under `dbus-run-session`, with `HOME=tests/sandbox/home`, its own `XDG_*` folders and
runtime folder (`tests/sandbox/run`), and `QT_PLUGIN_PATH` and `QML_IMPORT_PATH` pointing at the sandbox's home first.
KWin runs SCENARIO as its session and exits with it. Nothing touches the real session, its settings or its D-Bus.

```bash
tests/sandbox/run.sh "$PWD/tests/sandbox/scenarios/quick-menu.sh" 200 > tests/sandbox/logs/run-quick-menu.log 2>&1
SANDBOX_SCALE=2 tests/sandbox/run.sh "$PWD/tests/sandbox/scenarios/readme.sh" 240   # the README's pictures, sharp
python3 -I assets/screenshots/make.py                                                # crops them into assets/
```

Pass the scenario's full path: KWin looks a bare name up in `PATH`. A scenario sources `prelude.sh` (starts
kactivitymanagerd and kded6, defines `shot NAME`, a Spectacle capture into `tests/sandbox/shots/NAME.png`, and
`waitfor SECONDS`), starts plasmashell or the app under test, drives it, captures, and writes PASS or FAIL lines to
`tests/sandbox/logs/<name>.txt` where it checks something. The home, captures and logs are not in git.

## Its home folder

The sandbox's home is a whole Plasma home (panels, caches, a browser profile), so it stays out of git. To give it the
theme's current files: `HOME=$PWD/tests/sandbox/home python3 -I installer/install.py files --no-session`.
`tests/sandbox/relayout.sh` rebuilds its panels from `layout.js` and copies the real tray's settings into it.

## Driving it

- `tests/helpers/fakeinput/fakeinput` speaks `org_kde_kwin_fake_input` to the nested KWin only: `move X Y`,
  `glide X Y STEPS`, `down`, `up` (left button), `rdown`, `rup`, `mdown`, `mup`, `keydown CODE`, `keyup CODE` (evdev codes: 125 Win, 28 Return, 1 Esc,
  103/108/105/106 arrows), `wait MS`.
- `tests/helpers/region_changed.py BEFORE AFTER X0 Y0 X1 Y1` exits 0 when a region changed (mean difference above 6):
  the usual "did it open" check. Keep the region tight around what appears.
- `tests/helpers/fake-tray` puts tray icons in the nested tray (`tray_apps.sh`); `fake_mpris.py` plays a track.
- KWin scripts print into KWin's output, which is the run log.

## Gotchas

- Plasma's menu is `plasma-applications.menu`: export `XDG_MENU_PREFIX=plasma-` and run `kbuildsycoca6
  --noincremental` in scenarios that need the app catalog (Quick Menu, launchers).
- The sandbox's activity statistics stay empty even with a copied database, so Quick Menu's Suggestions show only live.
- KWin keeps the sandbox screen's saved scale; `readme.sh` sets the scale it needs with `kscreen-doctor` and puts 1 back.
- Wayland dismisses a popup that no real input opened: capture QWidget menus from an X11 client
  (`QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb`, `explorer-menus.sh`).
- An active fullscreen window covers the panel; QML `Item.left/top` are FINAL; a DropArea inside a ToolTipArea never
  gets drags; libplasma prefers an applet's compiled QML over a package on disk.
- A click outside a popup closes it: color searches for click targets must stay inside the panel.

[Aurora](../README.md) / [Documentation](index.md) / Releasing

# Versions and releases

Aurora follows [Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html) and keeps its history in
[CHANGELOG.md](../CHANGELOG.md) in the [Keep a Changelog 2.0.0](https://keepachangelog.com/en/2.0.0/) format. Commits
follow [Conventional Commits 1.0.0](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/). Each version gets a git tag
`vX.Y.Z` and a GitHub release with a source archive that installs without git.

## What the version number promises

The version covers what a user installs and uses: `./install.sh` and `./uninstall.sh` and their options, the ids and
folders written to the home folder (`org.aurora.*`, `~/.local/share/aurora`, `~/.local/state/aurora`), and the
settings the install changes and the backup restores.

| Change | Version |
| --- | --- |
| A fix that changes nothing a user relies on | patch: 1.0.0 → 1.0.1 |
| A new part, option or behavior, compatible with what is installed | minor: 1.0.1 → 1.1.0 |
| Renamed ids or folders, a removed option, anything that needs a fresh install or that an older backup cannot undo | major: 1.1.0 → 2.0.0 |

A supported Plasma version is not part of the promise: the parts build for whatever Plasma 6 is installed.

## Day to day

1. Commit with a Conventional Commits message: `feat(quick-menu): drag apps within a section`,
   `fix(installer): keep the Dock's pinned apps`, `docs: …`, `test: …`, `chore: …`; `feat!:` or a
   `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer for a major change.
2. In the same change, add what a user would notice to `## [Unreleased]` in CHANGELOG.md, under one of the six types:
   Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security. Write it for the user, not as the commit message; mark a
   breaking entry with **Breaking:**. Internal changes (tests, refactors, docs) need no entry.
3. `git-cliff --unreleased --strip all` ([cliff.toml](../cliff.toml)) drafts entries from the commits since the last
   tag when a lot has piled up; it is a draft to curate, not the entry.
4. `python3 -I scripts/changelog.py check` checks the format; `scripts/check.sh` runs every test.

## Cutting a release

```bash
scripts/release.sh 1.1.0             # checks, dates the changelog, commits, tags, builds the files and the package
scripts/release.sh 1.1.0 --publish   # the same, then pushes, creates the GitHub release and publishes the repository
```

This is the only way a version goes out. Every step below runs every time, and a failing one stops the release
before anything leaves the PC: no tag is pushed and no release is created for a package that failed its checks.

`scripts/release.sh` refuses a dirty tree, a version that is not SemVer or not above the last one, a changelog out of
format, an empty `[Unreleased]`, and a failing check. Then it:

1. moves `[Unreleased]` into `## [1.1.0] - YYYY-MM-DD` and relinks the versions to their comparisons;
2. writes `VERSION`, commits `chore(release): 1.1.0` and tags `v1.1.0` with the release notes;
3. builds `build/release/1.1.0/`: `aurora-1.1.0.tar.gz` (the sources and the themes),
   `release-notes.md` (the version's changelog section) and `SHA256SUMS`;
4. writes the AUR package for that archive in `build/release/1.1.0/aur/`: `PKGBUILD` and `aurora-theme.install` from
   [packaging/aur](../packaging/aur) with `pkgver=1.1.0`, `pkgrel=1` and the archive's SHA-256, and `.SRCINFO`;
5. builds the package into `build/release/1.1.0/repo/` with [scripts/pacman-repo.sh](../scripts/pacman-repo.sh): in
   the clean chroot, started on an older processor and checked against `aurora update` (section "Every x86-64
   processor" below);
6. with `--publish`, pushes the branch and the tag, runs `gh release create v1.1.0` with those files and notes, then
   publishes the repository built in step 5 (`pacman-repo.sh --publish-built`) and checks it the way a user's pacman
   sees it (next section).

Without `--publish` it prints the exact publish commands, so a release can be reviewed, package and checks included,
before anything leaves the machine. A failed step leaves the release commit and tag on this PC only:
`git tag -d v1.1.0 && git reset --hard HEAD~1` takes them back. Afterwards, copy `build/release/1.1.0/aur/` (`PKGBUILD` and `.SRCINFO`) into `packaging/aur` and commit it
as `chore(packaging): AUR package for 1.1.0`, so the repository's package names the latest release. The release flow is tested in [tests/release/test_release.sh](../tests/release/test_release.sh).

## The pacman repository

Users install `aurora-theme` from Aurora's pacman repository: the files of the GitHub release tagged `repo`, which
[get.sh](../get.sh), README.md's one-command [Installation](../README.md#installation), adds to pacman.conf as
`[aurora]`. get.sh names the key's fingerprint, so a new key is changed there too. The release holds one version:
the package, the `aurora` database, their signatures and `aurora.asc`. Publishing uploads the package first, the
database that lists it next and removes the older build's files last, so the database online never names a missing
package. It refuses a package whose name the release already has: pacman caches packages by name, and makepkg never
builds the same bytes twice, so a rebuild raises `pkgrel`.

```bash
scripts/pacman-repo.sh build/release/1.1.0/aur build/release/1.1.0/repo             # builds and signs, publishes nothing
scripts/pacman-repo.sh build/release/1.1.0/aur build/release/1.1.0/repo --publish   # the same, then replaces the release's files
scripts/pacman-repo.sh build/release/1.1.0/aur build/release/1.1.0/repo --publish-built   # publishes what is built
```

After the upload, [scripts/verify-repo.sh](../scripts/verify-repo.sh) checks the repository as a user's pacman sees
it: a throwaway pacman that trusts only `aurora.asc`, as get.sh sets it up, starts from the database that was online
before the upload (saved with the server's time, so pacman asks only for a newer one, as on a PC that synced the last
release), syncs, and must see the new version, verify its signature and download the very file the checks passed.
A failure there means users would not get the release.

Everything is signed with Aurora's key. Its public half is [packaging/repo/aurora.asc](../packaging/repo/aurora.asc)
(fingerprint `657D8110799A4E65BE4E1AB4F028284112794CC2`), which users trust with `pacman-key --lsign-key`; its secret
half lives only in my GnuPG keyring and an offline copy, never in the repository. A new key means every user trusts
it again, so it is replaced only if the secret half is lost or exposed. `release.sh --publish` runs the script itself;
a change to the package alone (a new dependency) raises `pkgrel` and runs it by hand. The flow is tested in
[tests/release/test_pacman_repo.sh](../tests/release/test_pacman_repo.sh).

### Every x86-64 processor

The package is built on my PC and installed on everyone's, so it has to run on any 64-bit x86 processor, not only on
mine. Three things on this PC break that, and each one has shipped once:

| What leaks | How | Seen in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The compiler flags | CachyOS's makepkg.conf asks for the building PC's own processor (`-march=native`, `-C target-cpu=native`) | issue #11: "Illegal instruction" |
| Code of the toolchain | CachyOS's x86-64-v3 libgcc links `__popcountdi2` with `popcnt` | found while fixing #11 |
| The ISA mark | CachyOS's x86-64-v3 glibc marks its program start object (`/usr/lib/Scrt1.o`) as needing x86-64-v3; GNU ld and mold copy the mark into every program, and glibc's loader refuses to start it below that level | issue #14: "CPU ISA level is lower than required" |

glibc writes the mark into that object from the level glibc itself was compiled for, and its loader checks every
program and library against the processor before any of their code runs (glibc commit ecce11aa, "x86: Support
GNU_PROPERTY_X86_ISA_1_V[234] marker"). So no flag fixes the last two: the toolchain itself is built for a newer
processor. The fix is to build somewhere else.

1. **A clean chroot of Arch's packages.** [scripts/pacman-repo.sh](../scripts/pacman-repo.sh) builds a package with
   machine code only through [scripts/clean-build.sh](../scripts/clean-build.sh): devtools' `mkarchroot` and
   `makechrootpkg` (ArchWiki, "DeveloperWiki:Building in a clean chroot") in `build/chroot`, with Arch Linux's own
   core and extra ([packaging/repo/chroot-pacman.conf](../packaging/repo/chroot-pacman.conf), the architecture named
   `x86_64`, since CachyOS's pacman reads `auto` as x86_64_v3 too) and Arch's generic makepkg.conf from devtools.
   Every compiler, library and start object in it is built for the x86-64 baseline.
2. **A run on an older processor.** clean-build.sh then installs the package in the chroot and runs
   [scripts/old_cpu.py](../scripts/old_cpu.py): every program starts with the arguments of its line in
   [packaging/repo/old-cpu-runs.txt](../packaging/repo/old-cpu-runs.txt) and every library is loaded with dlopen,
   under QEMU's user mode as an AMD Opteron of 2003 (`Opteron_G1`: SSE2 and nothing newer), with Arch's Qt and KDE
   libraries, the ones a user has. A program without a line fails, so a new one cannot skip it. On the published
   1.3.0 package it fails File Explorer and krunner with the user's own message; the fixed build passes all ten.
3. **Checks of the files themselves.** In the package, `build()` adds `-march=x86-64 -mtune=generic` and
   `-C target-cpu=x86-64` after makepkg's flags (the last one wins in GCC and rustc; makepkg's hardening flags stay),
   ends with `cpu_baseline.py --relabel`, which marks a program whose code holds nothing newer than the baseline as
   needing only the baseline, and `check()` runs [scripts/cpu_baseline.py](../scripts/cpu_baseline.py) on the
   `aurora` command and every built part before they are stripped: an instruction newer than SSE2 is refused unless
   its function is built for that instruction set on purpose and named for it (memchr's `find_avx2`, which runs only
   after asking the processor), and so is a mark above the baseline. These keep an AUR build on a CachyOS PC right
   too, where no chroot is used.

4. **What `aurora update` installs.** The package is built against Arch's Plasma and a CachyOS user has CachyOS's
   rebuild of it. `aurora update` installs a new package only when the Plasma, KWin, Qt and KDecoration it was built
   for match the system's (cli/src/system.rs, `LINKS`), and waits otherwise. So clean-build.sh reads the package's
   `.BUILDINFO` and compares it with a fresh copy of every repository of this PC, CachyOS's and Arch's
   ([scripts/built_for.py](../scripts/built_for.py), by the same rules, read from that file). When Arch is ahead of
   CachyOS, the release waits for CachyOS.

The tests: [tests/release/test_cpu_baseline.sh](../tests/release/test_cpu_baseline.sh),
[tests/release/test_built_for.sh](../tests/release/test_built_for.sh), [tests/release/test_release.sh](../tests/release/test_release.sh),
[tests/release/test_pkgbuild.sh](../tests/release/test_pkgbuild.sh),
[tests/release/test_old_cpu.sh](../tests/release/test_old_cpu.sh) and
[tests/release/test_pacman_repo.sh](../tests/release/test_pacman_repo.sh) (a package with machine code is built only in
the clean chroot). The release build itself is the large test: it does not publish what fails on the Opteron or what
`aurora update` would not install.
A release needs `devtools` and `qemu-user-static`, and root through sudo once (SUDO_ASKPASS for a graphical prompt).

## Publishing to the AUR

The AUR has closed new accounts for now, so `aurora-theme` is not on it yet. When it reopens:

The package is [`aurora-theme`](../packaging/aur/PKGBUILD). It builds the `aurora` command, installs it to
`/usr/bin/aurora` and the theme's files to `/usr/share/aurora`; each user then runs `aurora`, which builds the parts
for their Plasma in `~/.cache/aurora/build` and installs into their home folder. After the GitHub release exists:

```bash
cd build/release/1.1.0/aur
makepkg -f && namcap PKGBUILD *.pkg.tar.zst   # builds from the published archive and lints the package
git clone ssh://aur@aur.archlinux.org/aurora-theme.git ../aur-repo   # once; the AUR account needs an SSH key
cp PKGBUILD aurora-theme.install .SRCINFO ../aur-repo/ && cd ../aur-repo
git commit -am "Update to 1.1.0" && git push
```

A change to the package alone (a new dependency) raises `pkgrel` in `packaging/aur/PKGBUILD`, then the same steps
with `makepkg --printsrcinfo > .SRCINFO`. The first upload needs the repository to be public, since the package
downloads its archive from the GitHub release.

## The GitHub page

- `python3 -I scripts/github_meta.py` shows the description and topics it would set; `--apply` sends them.
- The social preview, what a shared link shows on Discord, X, Reddit and the rest, is
  `assets/readme/social-preview.jpg` (`assets/readme/make.py` draws it). GitHub has no API for it: upload it under
  Settings, Social preview.
- The Apple logo among the menu bar logos is Apple's trademark; Simple Icons' drawing is CC0, the mark is not.

## Installing a release

```bash
tar -xzf aurora-1.1.0.tar.gz && cd aurora-1.1.0 && sha256sum -c ../SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing && ./install.sh
```

`./install.sh --version` prints the version a checkout or archive holds.

# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/2.0.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

The version covers what you install and use: the commands `./install.sh` and `./uninstall.sh` and their options,
the ids and folders the theme writes to your home folder (`org.aurora.*`, `~/.local/share/aurora`), and the settings
it changes. A change that needs a fresh install, or that an earlier backup cannot undo, is a major version.

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- File Explorer's address field shows the path as segments you can click, as Windows' File Explorer does; a click
  beside them, Ctrl+L or Alt+D still opens it for typing. In both the address field and the path bar, the arrow after
  a segment lists the folders inside it, the ellipsis of a long path lists the folders it hides, a middle click or
  Ctrl+click opens a segment in a new tab, and a right-click offers Open, Open in New Tab, Open Terminal Here, Copy
  Path and Get Info.
- Files dropped on a segment move, copy or link there (it asks which), or get the tag of a tag's shelf. A drag held on
  a segment opens that folder, so you can go on deeper. Dropping a folder into itself, or files into the folder they
  are already in, is refused. A segment dragged out carries its folder, to the sidebar, a tab or a terminal.
- Screen readers read File Explorer's path bar as one link per folder, which they can press.
- File Explorer's Edit menu has Undo (Ctrl+Z) for the last move, copy, rename, new folder or trash, named after it.
- File Explorer filters the folder on screen as you type (Ctrl+Alt+F, or More > Filter by Name): only the items whose
  names contain the text stay, with the number of matches beside it. Enter or the Down arrow goes to the first item,
  Escape shows everything again, and moving to another folder ends the filter.
- Renaming several items in File Explorer (F2) opens a Rename sheet with Finder's choices: replace a text (or a
  regular expression), add a text before or after the name, or give them one name with an index, a counter or each
  item's date, and also a change of case. Every new name shows before anything changes, a name that cannot be taken
  is marked with the reason, extensions stay, and one Ctrl+Z takes the whole batch back.
- File Explorer has a command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or More > Command Palette): a few letters find any command of
  its menus, shown with where it lives and its shortcut, and Enter runs it.
- File Explorer has an Inspector at the right of the files (Ctrl+Alt+I, or View > Show Inspector): a preview, the
  real size of folders and selections with the space they take on disk, kept current while it is open, where the
  item is, its dates, owner and permissions, and for a file its SHA-256, SHA-512, SHA-1 or MD5 with a field that
  says whether a pasted hash matches. Closed, it does nothing.
- File Explorer opens a zip, tar or 7z archive as a folder on a double click, as Windows' File Explorer does, with
  the path bar reading through the archive and Up leaving it for its folder. View > Open Archives as Folders turns it
  off; documents that are zips inside, like OpenDocument files, still open in their applications.
- In a Git repository, File Explorer and Dolphin show each file's Git status, and File Explorer's context menu has
  a Git submenu (Log, Add, Commit, Push and more). Aurora now installs `dolphin-plugins` for it and turns its Git
  plugin on, leaving any other plugin you turned on as it is.
- Smart folders: Save in File Explorer's search row keeps the search in the sidebar under a name you choose. It
  opens like a folder and stays current as files come and go; Dolphin lists it too, under Search For.
- File Explorer has Finder's columns view (the fourth view button, or View > as Columns): a column for each folder
  from your home folder down to the one you are in, with the files as the last column. A click in a column goes
  there, and you can drop files on a column's folders.
- File Explorer searches the whole PC as you type: a helper keeps an index of every local disk's names and answers
  in a few milliseconds (490,544 names: under 3 ms for a word). It runs only while File Explorer is used and leaves
  a few minutes after, catches up on what changed meanwhile without reading everything again, follows changes live,
  and shows each user only what that user may open. A scope row picks This PC or the folder; Everything's syntax
  works (`ext:`, `size:`, `dm:`, wildcards, `regex:`, `|`, `!`). Folders it does not index, like network shares, are
  searched as before. `aurora-search-query` asks it from a terminal.

### Changed

- Copy Path in File Explorer (Ctrl+Alt+C) copies the paths of every selected item, one per line, instead of only the
  first; with nothing selected it copies the folder's path.
- `aurora` looks for a newer Aurora when its menu opens, unless it looked in the last 5 minutes, so a new release
  shows up right away instead of after the next daily check.
- `aurora update` sets up Aurora's repository by itself when it needs it: when pacman.conf's `[aurora]` section is
  missing or points elsewhere, or pacman does not trust Aurora's key, it says so and fixes it with your password, so
  pacman always sees new versions. `aurora status` shows the repository's state.

### Fixed

- The menu no longer offers an older Aurora after you updated through pacman or paru. On 1.3.1 it still said
  "Aurora 1.3.0 is available".
- `aurora update` checks that pacman really installed the new version, and says how to retry when it did not.
- In File Explorer, the Move, Copy or Link menu of files dropped on the sidebar opens where they were dropped, not off
  to the side by the sidebar's offset in the window.

## [1.3.1] - 2026-11-08

### Fixed

- File Explorer and Quick Menu start on processors without AVX2, such as Intel Pentium, Celeron and Atom chips. The
  package's programs were marked as needing a newer processor, so the system refused to start them with "CPU ISA
  level is lower than required", and Quick Menu's key only showed "Launching KRunner failed".
- Building Aurora from its sources no longer stops at the pointing hand on a system without `vulkan-headers`, which
  KWin's build files ask for; the installer now installs it.

## [1.3.0] - 2026-11-07

### Changed

- The notifications popover in the menu bar looks like macOS Tahoe's Notification Center. Each notification sits on
  its own rounded glass card with the app's icon large at the left, a bold title with its time and the message below,
  and a picture in rounded corners at the right. Clear appears over a card's top-right corner on hover. The app's
  settings and Minimize moved to the menu of a right-click or the Menu key. Do not disturb reads as a settings row
  with its switch at the right, and the label also turns it on. An empty popover shows a bell with "No Notifications".
  A long message shows its first four lines and opens in full with a click or Show More, and older notifications
  show their date.
- Aurora's Mission Center is one sheet of dark glass like File Explorer: KWin blurs what is behind it, the device
  sidebar floats as the clearer glass, the pages switch in one glass capsule, the window buttons sit in another, and a
  window that is not in front turns opaque. The graphs are tinted cards, the Performance details sit on a glass card,
  and the Services filters are chips. The device sidebar now stays on Apps and Services too, when the window is wide
  enough for every column, and a click on a device opens its Performance view. The search field is always in the
  header bar, and typing on the Performance page searches the apps. Busy values in Apps and Services are tinted
  warmer as they rise, as in the Windows 11 Task Manager; Preferences and `aurora mission-center settings` turn the
  tint off.
- Mission Center's Apps and Services pages sit on a glass card with the column headings inside, the Apps and
  Processes headings no longer show as a grey selected bar, Stop, Force Stop and Details are separate glass pills, and
  busy cells get a rounded tint, blue for CPU and GPU and amber for memory. The device sidebar now fits beside every
  column from a 1220 px wide window. On Performance, each reading is a glass tile, two to a row, with the details on
  a card below, lined up with the graphs instead of starting under an empty gap. The selected device in the sidebar is
  glass instead of solid blue.
  Its header is File Explorer's toolbar: the window buttons sit in the same capsule with the same glyphs and at the
  same distance from the window's edges, every control has the same height on one line, and the sidebar and edit
  buttons sit at the sidebar's top left as in File Explorer, where the sidebar button stays when the sidebar is
  hidden. In a narrow window, or while the sidebar is being edited, the search field narrows so the page tabs keep
  their full names. The light style gets the same glass as the dark one instead of the old look.
  Its glass is now File Explorer's: the same tint over a real blur, the sidebar the clearer glass, and the same soft
  shadow drawn by KWin; the window resizes from just inside its edges. The devices in the sidebar, the tables and the
  graphs keep File Explorer's spacing from the edges instead of touching them.
  Its right-click menus, the main menu and tooltips are File Explorer's blurred glass with its row sizes, blue
  highlight, check marks and soft shadow, and submenus such as Send Signal open beside the menu instead of replacing
  it. Dialogs use File Explorer's dialog color, and Preferences is wide enough for its four page names. A drive's
  partitions sit on a glass card under its details, with File Explorer's capacity bars that turn amber past 90 % used
  and red past 95 %, and a network's addresses join the rest of its details on their card.
- The menu bar stays see-through over a maximized window, so its popups (notifications, sound, network) stay glass
  like File Explorer instead of turning solid gray.

### Fixed

- The menu bar's status icons drawn by Aurora (volume, network, media, the bell and the magnifier) show correctly in
  GTK apps. GTK drew their outlines filled, so Mission Center's search button showed a solid dot instead of a
  magnifier.
- Table headings in GTK apps line up with their columns again. Aurora's GTK theme padded them like list
  headers, which moved each heading to the right of its values and cut off the last one, such as Mission Center's
  GPU Memory.
- The window buttons of GTK apps are as sharp as File Explorer's. Their glyphs sat between two rows of pixels, so
  they looked dimmer and thicker.
- Mission Center's Performance details no longer run past the window's right edge in a narrow window.

## [1.2.0] - 2026-11-07

### Added

- Mission Center is part of Aurora. `aurora mission-center on` puts Aurora's build in place of the distribution's:
  each app's GPU, memory and network use counted exactly, a lean background service, fan readings that match the
  hardware and a color per device. It comes from Aurora's repository or is built on your PC; `off` puts the
  distribution's back. Every change saves a snapshot of the build and the settings first, and
  `aurora mission-center rollback` puts one back.
- `aurora mission-center settings` changes the refresh, the charts, the look, the graphs and the sidebar, and `--set`
  reaches any Mission Center setting, checked before anything changes. `aurora status` and `aurora settings` show it.

### Changed

- `aurora update` installs a new Aurora only in a way its parts keep working. It first reads which KDE Plasma, KWin,
  Qt and KDecoration the new package was built for, then updates it with the rest of the system when that is what a
  system update brings, on its own when it is built for the system as it is, and not at all when it fits neither,
  saying which versions differ. With no new Aurora out it changes nothing, where it used to update the whole system.
- `aurora update` installs the package from Aurora's repository with pacman instead of the AUR helper, so AUR packages
  are no longer rebuilt along with it.
- An inactive File Explorer window is opaque, as a macOS window is when it is not in front, so nothing behind it shows
  through, blurred or not. Its sidebar selection turns gray with it, like the selections in the file views.

### Fixed

- Aurora runs on every 64-bit x86 PC. The package was built for the processor of the PC that built it, so on
  a PC with an older processor `aurora` stopped with "Illegal instruction" right after the install, and its parts
  would have stopped KWin and the panel the same way
  ([#11](https://github.com/xt0n1-t3ch/Aurora-CachyOS-Theme/issues/11)). It is now built for any x86-64 processor,
  and the package refuses to build when anything in it needs a newer one.
- File Explorer's Group menu works again with Dolphin 26.08, which replaced the action it used: None, Name, Kind, Date
  Modified, Date Created, Size and Tags, with the current choice checked and kept per folder.
- File Explorer's address and search fields show one focus ring. Breeze no longer adds its own square-cornered frame
  around them when Ctrl+L, Alt+D or Tab focuses them.

## [1.1.1] - 2026-11-06

### Fixed

- The install no longer stops at its last step, "Look and panels", with `unfilled placeholder in layout.js` on a
  desktop that does not have Aurora's menu bar yet: a comment in the panel script was taken for a placeholder.
- Publishing a new version uploads the package before the database that lists it, so `pacman -Syu` never reads an
  `[aurora]` database that names a package not online yet.

## [1.1.0] - 2026-11-05

### Added

- File Explorer takes typed paths: click the path in the toolbar, or press Ctrl+L or Alt+D, and type. Subfolders drop
  down as you type, Tab completes like a shell, `~` is your home folder, Enter goes there (a file opens its folder with
  the file selected) and Esc puts the path back. A path that leads nowhere rings the field red.
- File Explorer's row of file actions under the toolbar: new folder, new file, Move to Trash, rename, duplicate, Quick
  Look, cut, copy, paste, Open Terminal Here and Split View.
- Quick Look: Space shows the selected file without opening it (pictures whole, text files, and a large preview with
  the kind, size and date for the rest); Space or Esc closes it, Enter opens the file.
- Split View (F3): two folders side by side in one tab; the toolbar and the path bar follow the one you work in.
- Finder's color tags: tag files from the context menu's color dots, the Tags submenu, the Edit Tags button or by
  dropping them on a tag in the sidebar. Tagged files show their colors as dots on their icons, in File Explorer and in
  Dolphin, and each tag in the sidebar lists its files. Tags are the standard `user.xdg.tags` attribute that Dolphin
  and Baloo also read.
- The sidebar's folders unfold: a folder you added shows a chevron that opens its subfolders, and Favorites,
  Locations and Tags fold away under their titles. Both are remembered.
- Quick Menu's All Applications: the grid button beside ⋯ lists every app once under its first letter, like Windows'
  All apps list, under a heading that reads like a section's, with Back where a section has Show More.
- The toolbar's Group menu (by name, kind, date modified or size), a Share menu, and a More menu with hidden files,
  previews, sort, Get Info and Add to Sidebar.
- Windows open, close, minimize and restore with Aurora Motion, a KWin effect in macOS's manner: a short scale and
  fade instead of the close that looked like the window was swallowed, and a minimize into its Dock icon. Quick Menu
  rises and fades in, the Control Center drops in, and File Explorer's hovers fade and its wheel scroll glides.
- `aurora settings` chooses the animation speed, smooth, fast or instant (`--animations` from a script), and applies
  it at once to the running desktop.
- `aurora performance on` and `off` turn the measured tuning on or back to CachyOS's settings at any time; alone it
  shows the four settings and whether they are in place.
- `aurora backups` lists the backups of your desktop from before Aurora, and `aurora backups restore` puts one back.
- `aurora icons` changes the icon theme to Aurora's or any other installed one, at once.
- `aurora settings` and the `aurora` menu reach every one of these.

### Changed

- The README's install, update, tuning and removal sections use the `aurora` command; the manual steps moved into
  folded sections.
- File Explorer's context menu follows Finder's order: Open, Open With, Open in New Tab; Rename, Duplicate, Compress
  to .zip, Quick Look; Cut, Copy, Copy Path, Paste; Move to Trash; the tags; Get Info, Quick Actions (the service
  menus) and Open Terminal Here, which opens a file's folder too.
- File Explorer's list shows Finder's columns in its order (Name, Modified, Size, Type) with 22 px icons, and the path
  bar at the bottom names the selected file after its folder, beside the item count and free space. The toggles of
  the old status row moved to the More menu and the View menu.
- Animations run at Plasma's designed speed (smooth, 1) instead of near-instant values.

## [1.0.0] - 2026-11-05

The first release: a macOS Tahoe-inspired desktop for CachyOS and KDE Plasma 6, installed with one command and one
question, and removed with one command.

### Added

- One command installs Aurora, in fish, bash or zsh: `curl -fsSL .../get.sh | bash` shows Aurora's wordmark, asks
  for your password once, adds Aurora's signed pacman repository, installs the aurora-theme package and opens
  `aurora`, whose only question is the menu bar's logo. The package comes with its parts built, so nothing is
  compiled on your machine, and every `sudo pacman -Syu` brings the new versions.
- Update notices: once a day (a user timer that catches up after the PC was off), Aurora looks for a newer version and
  offers it in a notification with Update now and Skip this version; `aurora` also names it above its menu.
  `aurora check-updates` looks right away.
- `aurora settings`: how often to look for updates (every day, every week or never; `--updates` sets it from a
  script) and the menu bar logo, so the install itself keeps its one question.
- Everything Aurora installs is in this repository: its themes, widgets and parts. Nothing is downloaded from other
  projects.
- `./install.sh` installs from the source in one go: the packages it needs, the eight compiled parts built for your
  Plasma, KWin and Qt, a backup of every setting it changes, and the look. Options: `--performance`, `--rebuild`,
  `--reset-panels`, `--check`, `--yes`.
- `./uninstall.sh` and `aurora uninstall` put back every saved setting and remove everything the theme added.
- The `aurora` command: the install with its one question, each step with its progress and a log, and `update`,
  `rebuild`, `logo`, `settings`, `check-updates`, `status` and `uninstall`. On the package, `aurora update` upgrades the
  whole system with it (`-Syu` through paru, yay or pacman), so there is never a partial upgrade.
- A license: Aurora's own code is free software under the GNU GPL version 3, with additional terms (NOTICE.md) that
  keep the author's credit in every version. `aurora license` shows them.
- File Explorer: a Finder-style file manager on Dolphin's engine, opened by Win+E, drawing every app's Open and Save
  panels and answering "Show in folder". Drag a row of its sidebar onto another of the same section to put Favorites
  and Locations in your own order; the order is kept.
- Window buttons: one glass capsule with minimize, maximize and close in Windows order, the same in Qt, GTK and
  libadwaita apps.
- Menu bar: the system menu under CachyOS's black-and-white logo (Arch Linux, Apple and Kali Linux are in its
  settings, each also in its own colors where it has them), the active app's name, the system tray with Windows 11
  drag and drop, Quick Menu, the Control Center and a macOS clock, in light text over the wallpaper.
- Quick Menu on the Windows key: macOS Tahoe's Applications view, and Plasma's search when you type. Drag an app onto
  another of its section to reorder the section; the order is kept. Right-click an app, or press the Menu key, to
  pin it to the top (a Pinned section above Suggestions) or to the Dock, remove it from Suggestions, edit it or
  uninstall it. Under Suggestions it also lists the app's recent files. Its rail, as in Windows 11's Start: your
  picture and name open Lock, Switch User and Log Out; the power button opens Sleep, Hibernate where the machine
  can, Restart and Shut Down.
- Control Center with Tahoe's floating glass modules, and notifications as macOS banners in the bottom-right corner.
- Dock with your pinned apps, Downloads and Trash, which steps aside for windows and comes back with one touch of the
  bottom edge.
- The pointing hand over everything clickable, KWin's window buttons included, and Aurora's cursors.
- Info Center > Energy: live CPU and GPU watts, a two-minute chart and the power profiles.
- Dawn Bird, Aurora's own wallpaper: a bird of folded glass rising at first light, in 5K, offered in the wallpaper
  picker.
- Aurora's colors, Plasma style, Kvantum and GTK themes, and icons with every app's own logo; the free Inter and
  JetBrains Mono fonts, or SF Pro and SF Mono when you installed them.
- `--performance`: the measured scx_lavd scheduler, memory and zram tuning.
- After a Plasma, KWin or Qt update, the parts built for the old version step aside on their own until the package
  brings them built for the new one; `aurora rebuild` builds them right away.

Source: docs/decisions.md (Decisions)

[Aurora](../README.md) / [Documentation](index.md) / Decisions

# Design decisions

The rules I set while building Aurora, and why. They decide every design question.

## Look and behaviour

- As beautiful as macOS Tahoe, with the habits of Windows, and no regression against the stock desktop (Dolphin's
  places, the tray's behaviour). Improvements are welcome, for example Windows 11 style drag and drop in the tray.
- Every design change is shown in real screenshots before it is applied.
- Window buttons: one minimalist glass capsule rather than traffic lights, in Windows order (minimize, maximize,
  close), the same size in Qt, GTK, libadwaita and the window decoration.
- Real app logos, and unique Settings, Downloads and Trash icons.
- Apps with their own design keep it (Edge, for one). The File Explorer design is for system surfaces: the Control
  Center, Open and Save panels, Win+E and the shell.
- No global menu in the top bar.
- The top bar and the Control Center reach macOS Tahoe's quality: smooth text, SF Symbols-like icons, macOS's order,
  and the date and time spaced as on macOS.
- Notifications are macOS banners, in the bottom-right corner where CachyOS puts them.
- Shortcut hints in menus are written the Windows way ("Ctrl+C"), never with Mac symbols.
- The Windows key alone opens Quick Menu, as Start does on Windows, drawn like Tahoe's Applications view. Its apps can
  be dragged within their category and keep that order. A right-click opens Open, the app's own actions, Pin to Top (a
  Pinned section above Suggestions, like Start's pinned apps), Pin to Dock, Remove from Suggestions, Edit Application
  and Uninstall; the Menu key and Shift+F10 open it from the keyboard.
- Quick Menu ends in a rail, as Windows 11's Start does: the account's picture and name open Lock, Switch User and Log
  Out; the power button opens Sleep, Hibernate (where the machine can), Restart and Shut Down. Plasma's session
  manager does the work, with its own confirmation.
- Power and Battery stays visible in the tray, where the power profile is switched.
- The pointing hand on everything clickable; the black minimalist macOS cursor elsewhere, GTK apps included.
- The clock follows the region's 12- or 24-hour format.
- The README's pictures show Orion first under Developer Tools and in the Dock.

## File Explorer's search index

- 2026-11-11, Tony: search must be instant, never stale, and cost nothing while it is not used, even with a File
  Explorer window open all day. Neither a resident indexer (Everything's way, always running) nor an index built
  when the window opens (a full read of the disks every time) meets that. The helper starts on demand from its
  socket, catches up from btrfs transaction ids or folder times instead of reading everything, follows changes with
  fanotify only while File Explorer is in use, and leaves when idle ([search.md](search.md)).
- The index lives in the helper's memory while it runs, not in a mapped file: entries link to each other and change
  in place, which a read-only mapping cannot hold, and the memory goes back when the helper leaves.
- `plocate`'s nightly `updatedb` stays: other programs use `locate`, and turning it off is the user's choice.

## Fonts

- Aurora ships only free fonts: Inter for the interface and JetBrains Mono with Nerd Fonts' symbols for Konsole.
  Apple's SF Pro and SF Mono are free to download but not to redistribute: their license allows them only for mock-ups
  of interfaces for Apple's systems. When SF Pro or SF Mono is installed (the AUR's `apple-fonts`, for one), the
  install uses it instead; Inter is the closest free match, a little wider, with the same shapes and weights.

## Way of working

- Research before deciding; measure before tuning, and say what is inferred.
- No hardcoding of one case where a general rule exists.
- Everything stays instant under load.
- Validation is local; GitHub holds the repository and its releases.

## Naming and the repository

- The theme is called **Aurora**, written in plain words everywhere: no code names. Ids and paths say `aurora`
  (`org.aurora.decoration`, `org.aurora.glass`, `aurora-pointer`, `~/.local/share/aurora`).
- The repository is organized by category: `components/`, `cli/`, `themes/`, `installer/`, `packaging/`,
  `performance/`, `tests/`, `docs/`, `assets/`. Everything Aurora installs lives in this repository: no submodules and
  nothing downloaded from other projects. One command installs everything (`./install.sh`), one
  undoes it (`./uninstall.sh`), and the README lists every library and package it uses.
- Aurora is a macOS Tahoe-inspired theme, never presented as a copy.
- Pages and code read like a person wrote them: no AI-looking icons, badges, slogans or phrasing.
- Nothing personal goes into the repository: no saved desktop settings, no private screenshots, no keys.
- Every showcase picture (the README, the social preview) is taken on Dawn Bird, Aurora's own wallpaper in
  `themes/wallpapers/Aurora`, chosen among three original concepts. It was generated for Aurora with an image model,
  scaled to 5120x2880 with Real-ESRGAN (realesrgan-x4plus) and given a fine grain against banding. The sandbox
  scenarios set it through `tests/helpers/showcase_wallpaper.sh`. The install offers it in the wallpaper picker and
  leaves the wallpaper alone.

## Menu bar logo

- The menu at the left of the menu bar shows CachyOS's black-and-white logo by default, so it matches the rest of the
  bar. It is cscs's symbolic version of the official mark, which follows the bar's text color.
- The menu's settings offer Arch Linux, Apple and Kali Linux too, and the CachyOS and Arch Linux logos in their own
  colors; any other icon still works.

## Installing and releasing

- `./install.sh` stays the one implementation of the install. The `aurora` command (Rust, `cli/`) is a guided front
  end over it: it asks for the logo and the tuning, shows each step with a spinner, logs the output, and also updates,
  rebuilds, changes the logo, shows the status and uninstalls.
- Distribution: the package `aurora-theme`, built from the GitHub release archive and served from Aurora's own signed
  pacman repository in the GitHub release `repo` (`sudo pacman -Syu aurora-theme`, then `aurora`). The AUR closed new
  accounts in 2026 after waves of malicious packages, so a repository I host is the route that works today; the same
  PKGBUILD goes to the AUR when it reopens. `bunx` was considered and dropped: it needs an npm package and puts a JavaScript runtime in front of a KDE
  theme.
- Versions follow SemVer, the changelog Keep a Changelog 2.0.0, commits Conventional Commits; `scripts/release.sh`
  cuts a release and publishes only with `--publish`.
- Everything a package ships prebuilt targets the x86-64 baseline, never the processor of the PC that builds it: the
  package is built once and installed on PCs older than mine. The speed a newer instruction set would add to a theme
  is not worth a desktop that stops with "Illegal instruction" (issue #11). Libraries that pick a faster path after
  asking the processor (memchr's AVX2 search) keep doing so.

## License

- Aurora must always credit its author. Aurora's own code is GPL-3.0-only with additional terms under its section 7
  (NOTICE.md): (b) keep the author attribution in the source and in the Appropriate Legal Notices of every
  interactive interface, (c) mark modified versions as such, (d) no use of the author's name to promote them.
  Section 5(d) already makes every modified version keep showing those notices, and `aurora license` plus the banner
  are where Aurora shows them.
- GPL rather than Apache-2.0 or MIT: those let a modified version keep the credit only in a NOTICE or license file
  and close its source; the GPL keeps every version open and, with 7(b), keeps the name in the interface. The
  Attribution Assurance License forces a splash screen on every launch, which no GPL code may be combined with, and
  Aurora is built on KDE's GPL code. "Only" rather than "or later" keeps the additional terms tied to the version
  they were written for.
- Every file of Aurora's own code carries a three-line header; `scripts/license_headers.py` adds and checks it.

# Aurora: copyright, license and attribution

**Aurora by xt0n1** ([github.com/xt0n1-t3ch](https://github.com/xt0n1-t3ch)).

License version 3 ([LICENSE](LICENSE)), together with the additional terms below. Every file of Aurora's own code says
so in its header (`SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0-only` and a line pointing here). It comes with no warranty, to the
extent permitted by law; see sections 15 and 16 of the license.

## Additional terms (GNU GPL version 3, section 7)

These terms supplement the GNU GPL version 3 for the files whose header points to this notice, and for every work
based on them.

1. **Author attribution, section 7(b).** Keep the author attribution
   "Aurora by xt0n1 (https://github.com/xt0n1-t3ch)" in the source files that carry it, and in the Appropriate Legal
   Notices of every interactive interface of the work: today the `aurora` command's banner ("Developed by xt0n1")
   and its `license` command. As section 5(d) allows, a modified version may change where and how those notices appear, as long as
   they still name the author.
2. **Modified versions, section 7(c).** Do not present a modified version as the original. Mark it in a reasonable
   way as different from it, for example "based on Aurora by xt0n1", so nobody credits the author with changes they
   did not make, or blames them for those changes.
3. **The author's name, section 7(d).** The name "xt0n1" may not be used to promote a modified version, or to
   suggest the author endorses it, without the author's written permission.

## What else is in this repository

The parts that come from other projects keep their own license: each file's header, or the license file in its
folder, is the final word.
